tools.name: BANKSY niches
tools.author: PointillViz reference tools
tools.description: Tissue niches from each cell’s expression and its neighbourhood’s, by the BANKSY method.
tools.readme_html:
Answers the question: Which tissue domains, or niches, does a section divide into, judged by what each cell and its neighbours express?

BANKSY (Singhal, Chou, Lee et al., Nature Genetics 2024) describes every cell by its own expression together with the expression around it, and clusters the cells on that joint description. With most of the weight on the neighbourhood, the clusters are tissue domains; with little, they are cell types refined by their surroundings.

What you get

  • Map. Every cell painted by its niche, one colour per niche. Niches are numbered N1, N2, … from the largest, and the numbers carry no other order. Cells without spatial neighbours, or outside a selection, are left unpainted.
  • Matrix. Each niche’s cell-type composition when the dataset has cell types; its marker genes otherwise.
  • Table. Each niche’s size, its five strongest marker genes and its three main cell types.
  • Download. A CSV (gzip) of every cell’s niche, when it fits in the result.

On a Xenium 5K mouse colon section of 135,000 cells, the defaults give 8 niches that follow the structure of the gut wall: the muscle layers, the lamina propria, crypt and surface epithelium, and a small niche of lymphoid aggregates (ILC3s and dendritic cells, with Cxcl13 and Ltb).

Parameters

  • Clustering. Leiden, the authors’ default, finds as many niches as the resolution calls for. k-means divides the cells into exactly the number of niches you ask for.
  • Resolution (Leiden). Higher values give more, smaller niches; lower values give fewer, larger ones.
  • Niches (k-means). How many niches k-means makes.
  • Neighbourhood weight (λ). 0.8 finds tissue domains, 0.2 spatially informed cell types, and 0 ignores space.
  • Spatial neighbours (k). How many nearest cells make a neighbourhood. The gradient features use twice as many.
  • Include gradients (AGF). Adds BANKSY’s azimuthal Gabor filter, which responds where expression changes across a neighbourhood, as at a border.
  • Variable genes. How many of the most variable genes to use. More genes take longer.
  • Principal components. How many components of the joint matrix the clustering sees.
  • Smooth labels. Gives a cell the niche held by more than half of itself and its 15 nearest cells, repeated until nothing changes (BANKSY’s smoothLabels).

Method

For each cell, three blocks over the most variable genes, ranked by dispersion as in scanpy’s flavor="seurat":

  • own: the cell’s library-size-normalised expression;
  • neighbourhood mean: a Gaussian-weighted average over its k nearest cells, the kernel scaled by the cell’s median neighbour distance;
  • gradient (AGF): the azimuthal Gabor filter over its 2k nearest cells. It is large where expression changes across the neighbourhood.

Each column is z-scored, the blocks are weighted by √(1−λ), √(2λ/3) and √(λ/3) (√(1−λ) and √λ without the gradient), and the joint matrix is reduced to its top principal components. The components are then clustered:

  • Leiden, as the authors’ Python package runs it. Each cell is linked to its 50 nearest cells in component space, with weight 1/(1 + distance). A link is kept when the two cells share five or more of those neighbours, or when it is one of the three links the cell shares the most neighbours over. Leiden (RBConfiguration quality, seed 1234, repeated until no cell moves) partitions this graph.
  • k-means, with k-means++ seeding and the best of four fixed starts. The authors’ R package offers it too (clusterBanksy(algo = "kmeans")).

The joint matrix is streamed in chunks rather than stored, so memory stays near the size of its Gram matrix, and the chunks are built on up to 16 processors.

This is a reimplementation in NumPy and SciPy, with python-igraph and leidenalg for Leiden. It takes no code from the authors’ packages. On that section, its three feature blocks match pybanksy 1.3.5 to within 5 × 10⁻⁸, and its principal components are exact, where pybanksy‘s default randomized PCA is unseeded and changes slightly from run to run.

Citation

Singhal V, Chou N, Lee J, et al. BANKSY unifies cell typing and tissue domain segmentation for scalable spatial omics data analysis. Nature Genetics 56, 431–441 (2024).
tools.citation: Singhal V, Chou N, Lee J, et al. BANKSY unifies cell typing and tissue domain segmentation for scalable spatial omics data analysis. Nat Genet 56, 431-441 (2024).

tools.name: Categorical Chords
tools.author: PointillViz reference tools
tools.description: Explore spatial contacts or shared membership between categorical annotations with count-weighted ribbons and enrichment colors.
tools.readme_html:
Answers the question: Which categorical groups occur together more or less often than expected?

The tool compares categorical annotations such as cell types, clusters, or spatial niches. It offers two analysis modes:

  • Spatial contacts counts pairs of cells from the same section that lie within the selected radius.
  • Annotation relationships compares two categorical annotations assigned to the same cells, without using spatial coordinates.

For each pair of groups A and B, the tool compares the observed count O(A,B) with the expected count E(A,B):

score(A,B)=log2(O(A,B)+1E(A,B)+1)

The expectation is calculated from the group frequencies within each section. In annotation mode, E(A,B)=n(A)n(B)/N. In spatial-contact mode, it represents the number of A-to-B pairs expected if the group labels were randomly redistributed over the observed cell positions. A score of 0 indicates agreement with the expectation; positive values indicate enrichment and negative values depletion.

Chord. Each sector represents one group. Ribbon width shows the observed number of cells or spatial pairs connecting two groups, while ribbon color shows their log2(O/E) score: orange indicates enrichment and blue depletion. The display limits affect only the chord diagram, which shows the most abundant groups and best-supported relationships.

Matrix. Both axes list the selected groups, and each square shows the corresponding log2(O/E) score. The matrix retains all group combinations, including those omitted from the chord diagram.

Table. Each row represents one group pair. Count gives the observed number of cells or spatial pairs, Expected gives the expected count, and log2 O/E shows the enrichment or depletion.

tools.name: Cell-Type Co-occurrence
tools.author: PointillViz reference tools
tools.description: Which cell types are found near each other more often than expected by chance.
tools.readme_html:
Answers the question: Which cell types are found near each other more often than expected by chance?

Both axes list all groups in the selected annotation, so each square represents one group pair. Its color shows the co-occurrence score within the selected radius: orange to light yellow indicates more neighboring pairs than expected under random mixing, while blue indicates fewer pairs than expected. The matrix is symmetrical, and its diagonal shows whether cells from the same group cluster together.

More specifically, the score is the log2-transformed ratio between the observed and expected numbers of neighboring cell pairs:

score(i,j)=log2(observed(i,j)+1expected(i,j)+1)

The observed value is the number of pairs from groups i and j found within the selected radius. The expected value represents random mixing and is calculated as:

expected(i,j)=2×Npairs×pi×pj

Here, Npairs is the total number of neighboring pairs, while pi and pj are the overall proportions of the two groups. Thus, a score of 0 means that there are as many observed pairs as expected, while scores of +1 and +2 indicate approximately 2× and 4× the expected number, respectively.

Sweeping the radius

The radius can be swept: the tool’s panel offers Sweep from … to … in … steps under the Radius control. Run sweep runs the tool once per radius, all in one process, and a slider then moves between the results — the matrix and the table at each radius, every one the tool’s own answer at that radius, with nothing re-run while you drag. Seeing every radius, not only the one that looked best, is the point: a pair that is enriched at one radius and not at its neighbours is a pair to distrust.

parameters.label: Radius

parameters.help: Selects the annotation used to define the groups being compared. Defaults to the cell-type column.

tools.name: Cell-Type Percolation
tools.author: PointillViz reference tools
tools.description: Whether a cell type is one connected mass or many islands.
tools.readme_html:
Answers the question: Which cell types form one connected structure, and which are split into separate patches?

For each group in the selected annotation, two cells are connected when they are no more than a distance r apart. Connections can form chains: if cell A is connected to B and B to C, all three belong to the same patch. As r increases, smaller patches merge into larger structures.

Map. Each cell is colored by the log10 size of its connected same-group patch at a fixed linking distance. Brighter colors indicate larger patches, darker colors indicate smaller patches, and unpainted cells have no result.

Plot. The x-axis shows the linking distance r, normalized by the typical nearest-neighbor distance within each group. The y-axis shows the fraction of the group’s cells contained in its largest connected patch.

Pc(r)=cells in the largest patchall cells in group c

Each line represents one group. Curves rising further to the left indicate greater connectivity, while curves rising further to the right indicate greater fragmentation.

Table. The percolation threshold r* is the smallest distance at which the largest patch contains the selected fraction of the group, 50% by default. r*/NN expresses this threshold relative to the group’s own spacing. r*/null compares it with random groups of the same size: values below 1 indicate greater connectivity than expected, while values above 1 indicate greater fragmentation.
tools.citation: Stauffer, D. & Aharony, A. (1994). Introduction to Percolation Theory, 2nd ed. Taylor & Francis. Gower, J. C. & Ross, G. J. S. (1969). Minimum spanning trees and single linkage cluster analysis. Applied Statistics 18(1), 54-64.

tools.name: Conditional Contact Odds
tools.author: PointillViz reference tools
tools.description: How much one extra neighbour of type B changes the odds a cell is type A, holding every other type’s neighbour count fixed.
tools.readme_html:
Answers the question: Which group pairs remain associated after the complete composition of each cell’s neighbourhood is taken into account?

The tool is based on a softmax model that relates each cell’s group identity to the composition of its local neighbourhood. The probability that cell i belongs to group A is modeled as:

P(z(i)=A|N(i))=softmax(h(A)+∑J(A,B)×N(i,B))

Neighbourhoods are defined by an undirected k-nearest-neighbour graph, and N(i,B) is the number of group-B neighbours connected to cell i. The model jointly estimates the group-specific offsets h(A) and the coefficients J(A,B) from the observed group labels. While h(A) accounts for the baseline tendency of a cell to belong to group A, the main quantities of interest are the coefficients J(A,B). They describe the association between groups A and B after the complete neighbourhood composition has been taken into account.

More precisely, while all other neighbour counts remain fixed, one additional B-neighbour changes the log-odds of group A versus group C by J(A,B)−J(C,B).

Map. Using the fitted softmax model above, each cell is colored by logP(z(i)=observed group|N(i)), the log probability assigned to its observed group, given its neighbourhood. Values closer to 0 indicate that the model assigns a high probability to the observed group, while more negative values indicate that the cell’s identity is unusual for its neighbourhood.

Matrix. Both axes list all groups, and each square shows the corresponding fitted coefficient J(A,B). The coefficients are centered to have a mean of zero, J′(A,B)=J(A,B)−mean(J). Positive values indicate stronger-than-average conditional association; negative values indicate weaker association or relative avoidance. The diagonal shows conditional self-association.

Table. Each row represents one group pair. Conditional log-odds is the centered J(A,B) value from the matrix. Marginal log2 obs/exp is the Cell-Type Co-occurrence score calculated on the same neighbour graph, without accounting for other groups. Contacts is the number of observed connections between the groups. Rank shift shows how the pair’s position changes when pairs are ranked by conditional association instead of ordinary co-occurrence. A positive value means that the pair ranks higher by conditional association, while a negative value means that it ranks lower.

tools.name: Expression Hotspots (Getis-Ord Gi*)
tools.author: PointillViz reference tools
tools.description: Where one gene forms clusters of high or low expression.
tools.readme_html:
Answers the question: Where does a selected gene form spatial clusters of high or low expression?

For a selected gene, the tool considers each cell together with its k nearest neighbours and calculates a Getis-Ord Gi* z-score. This score measures whether gene expression in that local neighbourhood is higher or lower than expected if the observed expression values were randomly distributed across the cells.

More specifically, the Gi* score expresses the difference between the observed and expected neighbourhood expression in units of the variation expected under random mixing:

Gi*=observed local expression − expected local expressionexpected random variation=∑j∈Nixj−mix¯Smi(n−mi)/(n−1)

Here, Ni contains cell i and its k nearest neighbours, mi is its size, xj is the selected gene’s expression in cell j, and x¯ and S are its mean and standard deviation across all n mapped cells.

Map. Each cell is colored by its Gi* z-score. Red shows locally elevated expression, while blue shows locally reduced expression. Because Gi* includes the cell itself, the map describes the expression level of the whole local region rather than whether one cell differs from its neighbours.

Summary. Gi* z-scores are converted into two-sided p-values and corrected across cells using the Benjamini–Hochberg method by default. Click the info icon after the run to see how many cells were classified as significant hotspots or coldspots at the selected q-value threshold.

Table. Each row represents one cell type. In hotspot and In coldspot count its cells in significant regions. Hotspot fraction gives the proportion of that cell type found in hotspots, while Mean Gi* shows its average hotspot score.
tools.citation: Getis & Ord (1992) Geographical Analysis 24(3):189-206; Ord & Getis (1995) Geographical Analysis 27(4):286-306.

tools.name: Interface Coherence
tools.author: PointillViz reference tools
tools.description: Whether two cell types meet along one front or in specks.
tools.readme_html:
Answers the question: Which group pairs form long, continuous boundaries rather than many short, disconnected contacts?

To identify boundaries between groups, the tool first connects the cells in each section using a Delaunay triangulation. Three cells form such a triangle if a circle can pass through all three centers without enclosing another cell center.

When two connected cells belong to different groups, the tool creates a small boundary piece between them, perpendicular to the line connecting their centers. Touching boundary pieces are combined into one segment when they separate the same two groups.

For each group pair, the tool measures the lengths s(1),…,s(q) of its separate boundary segments and summarizes them as:

Lw=∑ss2∑ss

Because segment length is used as a weight, long connected boundaries contribute more than short contacts. The same value is calculated after repeatedly shuffling the group labels while keeping cell positions fixed. Coherence is then:

C(A,B)=log2(Lw(observed)Lw(shuffled))

0 indicates the shuffled expectation, while +1 indicates an observed value about 2× as large.

Map. Cells along group boundaries are colored by their local coherence value. This is calculated similarly to C(A,B), but uses the lengths of the specific segments touching the cell instead of the pair-wide observed Lw. Cells on longer, more continuous segments than expected appear yellow, whereas cells on shorter, more fragmented segments appear blue.

tools.description: How crowded the tissue is around every cell.
tools.readme_html:
Answers the question: How densely are cells packed around each individual cell?

For each cell i, the tool measures the distance ri to its k-th nearest neighbour within the same section. tools.name: Mclust niches
tools.author: PointillViz reference tools
tools.description: Niches from the mix of cell types around each cell, fitted by a Gaussian mixture with mclust in R.
tools.readme_html:
Answers the question: Which kinds of surroundings do the cells sit in, judged by the cell types around them?

Describes every cell by the mix of cell types among its nearest cells, and groups cells with similar mixes into niches with a Gaussian mixture model (mclust). It is a native R tool: the analysis is plain R, and PointillViz hands it the cell types and the neighbours.

What you get

  • Map. Every cell painted by its niche, one colour per niche. Niches are numbered N1, N2, … from the largest, and the numbers carry no other order. Cells with no labelled neighbour, or outside a selection, are left unpainted.
  • Table. Each niche’s size and its three main cell types, as shares of the niche’s own labelled cells.

Parameters

  • Neighbours (k). How many nearest cells make up the mix around a cell. Neighbours are found within each cell’s own section.
  • Niches. How many niches the mixture model makes. If two niches hold the same cell types, ask for fewer.
  • Random seed. Chooses the 2,000 cells the mixture is fitted to. Change it to see how stable the niches are.

Method

  1. For every cell, the share of each cell type among its k nearest cells. Unlabelled neighbours are not counted.
  2. prcomp reduces the shares to at most 10 principal components. Directions with almost no spread are dropped: the shares sum to one, so the last direction carries nothing.
  3. mclust::Mclust fits a Gaussian mixture with one covariance shared by all niches (model “EEE”) to 2,000 cells drawn with the seed. Fitting on a sample keeps the run short, because mclust starts from a hierarchical clustering whose cost grows with the square of the number of cells.
  4. The fitted mixture gives every cell its most likely niche (predict).

On a Xenium 5K mouse colon section of 135,000 cells, the default niches follow the layers of the gut wall: stem and transit-amplifying cells at the crypt base, mature enterocytes at the surface, and smooth muscle with interstitial cells of Cajal and glia in the muscle layers.

Citation

Scrucca L, Fop M, Murphy TB, Raftery AE. mclust 5: clustering, classification and density estimation using Gaussian finite mixture models. The R Journal 8(1), 289–317 (2016).
tools.citation: Scrucca L, Fop M, Murphy TB, Raftery AE. mclust 5: clustering, classification and density estimation using Gaussian finite mixture models. The R Journal 8(1), 289-317 (2016).

tools.name: Neighborhood Composition & Mixing
tools.author: PointillViz reference tools
tools.description: How mixed each cell’s neighbourhood is, and who sits next to whom.
tools.readme_html:
Answers the question: How mixed is each cell’s neighbourhood, and which groups occur next to one another more or less often than expected?

For each cell i, the tool finds its k nearest neighbours and records how many belong to each group.

Map. Each cell is colored by the normalized Shannon entropy of its neighbourhood:

Mi=−∑jpijlog(pij)log(T)

Here, pij is the proportion of cell i’s labelled neighbours belonging to group j, and T is the number of groups present in the dataset. A score of 0 means that all labelled neighbours belong to the same group. Higher values indicate that several groups are represented more evenly.

Matrix. Both axes list all groups. Each square compares the observed number O(A,B) of A-to-B neighbour relations with the expected number E(A,B):

score(A,B)=log2(O(A,B)+1E(A,B)+1)

A score of 0 means that the observed and expected numbers match. Scores of +1 and −1 indicate approximately twice and half the expected number, respectively.

The expected number is calculated by multiplying the total number of valid neighbour positions around all A-cells (usually about n(A) × k) by the proportion of valid neighbour positions across all groups occupied by B-cells. Because the calculation counts neighbour positions rather than unique cells, the same cell may be counted multiple times, depending on its position and how many other cells include it among their k nearest neighbours.

Table. Each row summarizes one group. Cells scored is the number of its cells with a valid mixing score, while Mean mixing is their average Mi. Self log2 O/E is the group’s diagonal matrix value and indicates whether its cells cluster together or are more dispersed. Most enriched neighbour is the other group with the highest matrix score, and the accompanying log2 O/E column gives that score.

tools.name: Ripley’s Cross-L Function
tools.author: PointillViz reference tools
tools.description: At what distance cell type B accumulates around cell type A.
tools.readme_html:
Answers the question: At what distances does group B accumulate around or avoid group A?

The tool uses group A as the reference and measures the distances from its cells to cells from group B. It gradually increases a radius r around every A-cell and counts how many B-cells fall within that radius.

More specifically, let C(A,B)(r) be the number of observed A-to-B pairs separated by at most r. The cross-K function adjusts this count for the overall density ρ(B) of group B and for m(A)(r), the number of A-cells included at radius r:

K(A,B)(r)=C(A,B,observed)(r)ρ(B)m(A)(r) vs. C(A,B,expected)(r)ρ(B)m(A)(r)=πr2

Under complete spatial randomness, K(A,B)(r)=πr2. The tool transforms this comparison into a curve centered around zero:

L(A,B)(r)−r=K(A,B)(r)π−r

Positive values indicate more B-cells around A than expected, while negative values indicate fewer.

Plot. The x-axis shows the radius r, and the y-axis shows L(A,B)(r)−r. The solid line is the observed curve; its peak indicates the spatial scale at which B is most strongly accumulated around A. The grey band comes from random redistributions of the B labels while keeping A fixed. Values above the band indicate enrichment of B around A, while values below indicate spatial avoidance.

Table. Each row represents one tested radius r. L(r) − r is the observed curve value, while Envelope low and Envelope high are the lowest and highest values from the random relabellings at that radius. Outside envelope indicates whether the observed value lies above or below this range; a blank entry means that it lies inside.
tools.citation: Ripley, B. D. (1977). Modelling spatial patterns. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 39(2), 172-212.

tools.name: Tissue Permeability
tools.author: PointillViz reference tools
tools.description: Which cells one cell type seals off from the rest of the tissue.
tools.readme_html:
Answers the question: Which cells does one population seal off from the tissue surface or from another population?

The tool lets the user select one population as a potential barrier and choose a destination for the remaining cells: either the exposed tissue surface or another population. It then identifies which cells can no longer reach it when the barrier is impassable.

To identify possible routes through the tissue, the tool first connects the cells in each section using a Delaunay triangulation. Three cells form such a triangle if a circle can pass through all three centers without enclosing another cell center.

Multi-source Dijkstra routing calculates the shortest network distance to a source with the selected population passable, d(open)(i), and with it treated as impassable, d(barrier)(i). d(straight)(i) is the straight-line distance from cell i to the nearest source cell, ignoring the network.

A cell is sealed if it loses its route when the selected population becomes impassable. For cells that remain reachable, extra(i) measures the added network distance in median cell spacings s, while τ(i) compares the remaining route with the straight-line distance:

sealed(i)=[dopen(i)<∞ and dbarrier(i)=∞]
extra(i)=dbarrier(i)−dopen(i)s,τ(i)=dbarrier(i)dstraight(i)

Map. The user can choose between three display modes:

  • Sealed compartments colors only sealed cells. Dark colors indicate smaller compartments, while bright yellow indicates compartments containing more cells.
  • Extra path colors only reachable cells whose route becomes longer. Dark colors indicate a small additional distance, while bright yellow indicates that the barrier adds many cell spacings.
  • Detour factor colors only reachable cells with a valid τ(i)>1. Dark colors indicate a route close to the direct distance, while bright yellow indicates a much longer detour.

Plot. The x-axis shows cell percentiles after ranking by τ(i); at percentile q, the curve gives the detour factor that q% of the evaluated cells do not exceed. The y-axis shows τ(i), the network distance divided by the straight-line distance.

The red curve shows detour factors when the selected population is impassable, while the dashed curve shows the same tissue with it passable. The grey band shows the results when the same number of randomly selected cells are treated as barriers. If the red curve stops before the right edge, the missing percentage corresponds to sealed cells; their detour factors are non-finite and therefore not shown.

Table. Each row summarizes one population with at least 25 eligible cells, and Cells gives its total cell count. For the selected barrier and destination, Enclosed and % enclosed show the number and proportion of eligible cells that lose their route. Among cells that remain reachable, % detoured shows how often the route becomes longer, while Extra path where detoured gives the median number of cell spacings added to those longer routes. % enclosed, random barrier gives the average expected with equally large random barriers.

tools.name: Vector Field
tools.author: PointillViz reference tools
tools.description: Which way a quantity increases across the tissue, as arrows over the section. Gene, cell type or any annotation column — with every arrow that could be noise removed.
tools.readme_html:
Answers the question: In which direction does a selected quantity increase across the tissue, and how steeply?

The tool converts the selected quantity into a smoothed spatial field. Its gradient reveals the direction and strength of local changes across the tissue. Each cell j with a valid measurement receives a value aj. This is either the selected gene expression, a continuous measurement, or—for a selected population—1 for cells belonging to that population and 0 for other labelled cells.

At regularly spaced positions x across the tissue, the tool calculates a Gaussian-weighted local mean:

A(x)=∑jwj(x)aj,C(x)=∑jwj(x),F(x)=A(x)C(x)

The weight wj(x) decreases with the distance between cell j and position x, so nearby cells contribute more strongly to F(x) than distant cells. For a selected population, F(x) represents its smoothed local proportion.

From the spatial variation of this field, the tool calculates its gradient and magnitude:

∇F(x)=(∂F∂x,∂F∂y),g(x)=‖∇F(x)‖=(∂F∂x)2+(∂F∂y)2

Map. Cells are colored by the smoothed local value F(x): dark colors indicate lower values and yellow indicates higher values. The arrows show the gradient ∇F(x): their direction indicates the steepest increase, while their length represents the strength g(x) of the spatial change. For display, this strength is scaled nonlinearly as t(x)=min(g(x)/g95,1), where g95 is the 95th percentile of the displayed gradient magnitudes. Arrow color also represents F(x), not gradient magnitude.

Plot. To distinguish strong gradients from uncertain estimates, the tool calculates the effective cell count N(eff), the local variance τˆ2, and the standard error:

Neff(x)=(∑jwj(x))2∑jwj(x)2,τˆ2(x)=∑jwj(x)(a′j)2C(x)−(F(x)−a¯)2,SE(x)=τˆ(x)σp2Neff(x)

Here, a′j=aj−a¯ is the centered cell value, and σp is the spatial width of the Gaussian filter. A small effective cell count or high local variation increases the standard error. The x-axis shows a threshold t, while the y-axis shows the proportion of the M measurable positions whose standardized gradient magnitude z(x) reaches that threshold:

z(x)=g(x)SE(x),Sobserved(t)=1M∑x∈M1[z(x)≥t],Srandom(t)=e−t2/2

The solid curve shows the observed proportion. The dashed curve shows the frequency of standardized two-dimensional gradients expected from the Rayleigh distribution under random cell values. If the observed curve lies clearly above it, strong spatial gradients occur more often than expected by chance. The line at z=3 marks the default threshold below which arrows are hidden when filtering is enabled.
